did_you_know.text: Psalm 118 opens and closes with the same call: “Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; his steadfast love endures forever”—a structure that emphasizes the centrality of giving thanks for the LORD’s steadfast love.

In verses 2–4, the call to give thanks is addressed successively to Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear the LORD; in this way, the psalm brings different groups together as one community of worshipers giving thanks.

The phrase “from a place of distress” describes a place of pressure and trouble, while “into a spacious place” describes freedom and deliverance. The contrast between distress and spaciousness is central to the psalm’s description of salvation.
The psalm presents a clear comparison: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD” than “to trust in people”; in the next verse, the comparison is extended to trusting in princes as well.

The description of the enemies builds gradually: “All the nations surrounded me,” then “they surrounded me on every side,” and finally, “they surrounded me like bees.” The repetition creates a sense of being encircled from every direction.
In the tents of the righteous, “shouts of joy and salvation” are heard, and the verse links the joy of deliverance with the description of “the right hand of the LORD” as acting mightily.
The psalmist declares, “I will not die but live,” and explains the purpose of his life: “I will proclaim what the LORD has done.” Life is presented here as an opportunity to tell of the LORD’s deeds.

The request, “Open for me the gates of righteousness,” leads to a gate through which the psalmist can enter and give thanks; in the next verse, the gate is identified as the gate of the LORD, through which the righteous enter.
The image “The stone the builders rejected” describes something initially cast aside that becomes “the cornerstone”—a dramatic change from a position of rejection to one of central importance.

This verse contains a brief, twofold plea: “LORD, save us!” and “LORD, grant us success!” It is followed by a blessing on the one who comes in the name of the LORD, and finally by a renewed expression of thanks for his steadfast love.
